content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Before I build anything, I want to make sure I understand what you're really after — so let me start with the *why* rather than the *how*.

**When this bookmark app is finished and working well, what would be different from how you handle bookmarks today?** What's frustrating or missing right now that made you want to build this?

For example — are you drowning in a giant unorganized list, losing links you meant to come back to, wanting to share collections with others, or something else entirely? A little about how you picture using it day-to-day helps me understand the real goal behind "save and manage."

There's no wrong answer here — just tell me in your own words, and we'll shape it together from there.

Honestly, it's a mix of a few things that all add up.

Right now my links are scattered everywhere — some in my browser's bookmarks, some I text to myself, some just open in tabs forever because I'm scared I'll lose them if I close them. The browser bookmark bar becomes this giant messy pile and I can never find anything in it.

So the big thing is: I want one place where I save a link and actually *trust* I can find it again later. A couple of things that would make it feel "working well" to me:

- When I paste in a link, I don't want to sit there typing out what it is. It should kind of figure out the title and what the page is on its own, so my list is readable at a glance instead of just a wall of blue web addresses.
- I want to loosely group things — like "recipes," "work stuff," "articles to read" — without building rigid folders. And then just pull up everything in a group when I want it.
- Searching has to actually work. If I half-remember a link, I want to type a word and find it.
- A lot of what I save is "I'll read this later." So I'd love a way to mark those and see just my to-read pile separately, then check them off once I've read them.

Day to day, I picture it being fast: paste, it sorts itself out, and later I either search or click into a group and go. Does that give you enough to start shaping it?

- **The big one — should saving default *into* to-read?** You said "a lot of links come in that state by default for me." - **"Read" stays visible.** I chose to show a faint **✓ Read** badge on graduated links rather than hide the fact — so "done, but kept" is literally what you see. Say if you'd rather a read link show *no* marker at all.

**1 — Finding the pile.** The **📖 To read** chip set apart from my labels is right. It genuinely reads as a different *kind* of thing — a state, not a bucket — and the count with "to go" gives it that little checklist energy I wanted.

**2 — The satisfying part.** Ticking the circle and watching the link slide out and the count tick down — yes, *that's* the feeling. And then finding it still sitting in **All**, labels intact, wearing a quiet **✓ Read** — that's the "the pile shrinks but nothing is lost" I was after. Nailed it.

**3 — Undo.** Ticking the green circle to pop it back into the pile — yes, that safety net absolutely matters to me. I'll misfire and tick the wrong one, or realize I'm not actually done. Knowing I can just un-check it without hunting through menus means I'll trust the whole gesture. Keep it.

**4 — Getting things in.** Both ways work and both feel natural — the checkbox at save time for when I *know* I'm stashing to read, and the little **To read** button on a link later for when I change my mind. Good to have both.

On your assumptions:

- **The check-off gesture** — the circle right on the row is perfect. Immediate, no menu, no digging into Edit. Don't move it. Marking something read is a quick reflexive "done!" — it should live right where I'm looking.
- **Keeping ✓ Read visible** — yes, keep it. Hiding it would make a read link look identical to one I never touched, and I like *seeing* that I've been through it. "Done but kept" showing on the face of it is reassuring.
- **The big one — should saving default into to-read?** Here's my honest call: **no, keep it starting unticked, the way you have it.** I know I said a lot of my links come in wanting-to-read — and that's true — but not *all* of them. Sometimes I'm just filing a recipe I'm about to cook, or a reference I'll want later. If *everything* auto-landed in to-read, that pile would basically become "everything I've ever saved," and it'd lose all its meaning — the whole point is watching it *shrink* to zero, and that only works if it's things I actually mean to read. A pile I can never empty is just stressful.

That way when I hit a stretch of stashing reading material, I tick it once and it stays; when I'm just filing, I untick once and it stays. It adapts to me instead of forcing one rule. That's the best of both.

This rounds out all four of my original promises, and honestly they all feel good. Really pleased with where this landed.

Try these, in order:

**1 — The very first moment (empty state).** Before you touch anything, notice what an empty app says to you — the "Nothing saved yet 📎 / paste your first link" panel. Tell me if that feels welcoming and obvious for day one, or bleaves you unsure what to do.

**2 — The important one: a page it can't read.** Tick the dashed **"Simulate rough weather"** box, then paste any link and Save. Watch carefully. Tell me if what it does protects you — and whether it matches what you'd *want* to happen.

**3 — Compare.** Untick the box and save a normal link, so you can feel the difference between "read fine" and "couldn't read."

**4 — Gibberish.** Type something that isn't a link at all — like `asdf` — and hit Save. Tell me if how it responds feels right.

Here's what I decided, and where I most want your gut:

- **When it can't read the page, I chose to save it anyway** — with the web address standing in as the title, a clear "⚠️ couldn't read this — give it a name" flag, and a **Name it** button. My reasoning: the cardinal sin would be *losing* your link because a site was momentarily grumpy. Better to keep it and let you fix the name. But tell me — is "keep it, flag it, let me name it" right? Or would you rather it *tried again*, or refused to save until it worked?
- **Bad input gets a gentle inline nudge**, not a jarring popup — the box goes pink with a one-line explanation. Right touch, or too quiet?
- **The empty-state wording** — I wrote you a friendly first-run message; say if it should be warmer, plainer, or different.

And one honest gap I noticed while stress-testing that I should just ask you about plainly: **we've never talked about getting *rid* of a link.** When something's stale or you saved it by mistake — do you picture deleting it outright, and should a deleted link be truly gone, or recoverable in case you slip? No prototype yet — I just don't want to discover that hole later.

Good round — this is the kind of "what happens when things go wrong" stuff I wouldn't have thought to ask for, but it matters.

**1 — Empty state.** Welcoming and obvious. "Nothing saved yet, paste your first link" told me exactly what to do on a blank screen, and the little note that the title and summary fill themselves in is a nice reassurance up front. No confusion. Good day-one feeling.

**2 — The page it couldn't read.** This is exactly right, and it's the single most important call you've made all along: **keep it, flag it, let me name it.** Please don't change that. The one thing that would break my trust completely is pasting a link, walking away thinking it's safe, and finding out it silently vanished because a site hiccupped. Saving it with the address standing in, the clear ⚠️ flag, and a "Name it" button means my link is *never* lost — worst case I do a little tidying. That's the whole promise honored even on a bad day. (Trying again once quietly in the background before giving up would be a fine bonus — but if it still fails, *keep it*. Never refuse to save.)

**3 — The comparison** made the difference obvious — clean fill-in versus the flagged one. Clear.

**4 — Gibberish.** The gentle pink nudge with a plain one-line explanation is the right touch. A big alarming popup for a simple typo would feel like being scolded. This just quietly points and lets me fix it. Keep it that quiet.

Empty-state wording is fine as-is — friendly without being cutesy.

Now — the two honest gaps, because you asked plainly:

**On a page that goes bad for good.** Your "dead link" test poked at a worry I hadn't put words to. Right now if I save something and the page later *disappears entirely* — taken down, site gone — all I've got is a dead address that opens nothing. For links I really cared about, that's still losing the thing, just slowly. So I'll put the question to you: is there any way that what I saved keeps a bit of *the page itself*, not just a pointer to it — so if the original ever vanishes, I've still got something to look at? I don't know how hard that is, but "the link still works a year later even if the site died" is squarely part of "I trust I won't lose it" for me.

**On getting rid of a link — yes, and it's actually two different feelings:**

- Sometimes a link is genuine junk — I saved it by mistake, or it's a typo. That one I want to **delete outright, gone.** But — and you know me by now — I'm the nervous type, so a delete shouldn't be a hair-trigger. Give me a small "are you sure," or better, a brief "deleted — undo?" moment. A single misclick shouldn't permanently cost me something.

- But there's a second, softer case I care about just as much: a link that *isn't* junk — I'm just **done** with it, or it's cluttering my main list — and I don't want to throw it in the trash, I want to **tuck it away out of sight but keep it safe**, in case someday I need it again. That's not deleting. That's more like "file it away in the back room." I'd want those tucked-away links *out* of my normal list and search so they're not in my face, but still somewhere I can go dig them back out and un-tuck them.

So really: **delete = gone for good (with a small safety beat), and a separate "put it away" = hidden but recoverable.** Those are two different needs in my head, and I'd hate for them to be the same button. Glad you flagged the hole before we hit it.

cd implementation && python3 -m http.server 8000

Now let me guide you through confirming each thing we shaped — same as always, one action at a time. Please try each and tell me it behaves the way you approved:

**The everyday core**
1. **Paste & save** — drop in a real link. Watch the brief "figuring out…" then it fill in a title/summary, newest at the top. *(Honest note: to read the page it asks a helper service to fetch it; if that's blocked or you're offline, you'll see #6 instead — which is the point.)*
2. **Fix it** — click **Edit**, change the title, add a **note** in your own words, press **Done**. Then Edit again and press **Cancel** / **Esc** — confirm it backs out clean.
3. **Labels** — in Edit, add two labels to one link; type a partial one and confirm it offers an existing label to reuse (try a capitalized version of one you have — it should merge, not split). Click a label chip to pull up that pile.
4. **Search** — type two words that live apart in a link; confirm both light up. Search a word that's only in a **note**. Try `"quoted"` for exact.
5. **Read later** — tick "add to to-read" and save; open **📖 To read**; tick the circle to check one off and watch it leave the pile; find it still saved wearing **✓ Read**; tick again to undo.

**The safeguards**
6. **Never lost** — paste a made-up dead link (e.g. `https://nope.invalid/xyz`); confirm it's *still saved*, flagged "give it a name," never dropped.
7. **No duplicate** — save a link, save it again → it takes you to the one you have.
8. **Gibberish** — type `asdf`, Save → gentle pink nudge, no popup.
9. **Delete vs Put away** — in Edit, try **🗑 Delete** (then **Undo** in the bar) and **🗄 Put away** (then find it in the Put-away room and put it back).
10. **Sort** — flip Newest / Oldest / A–Z.
